reconcile.connective: Gill grants that afflictions really befall the righteous, then reclassifies them: since God overrules them for good, none of it counts as true "evil."

discrepancy.connective: Even Gill, a harmonizer, admits the prophet and "all good men" found real difficulty reconciling God's holiness with the wicked devouring the righteous.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Or the evil of punishment is here meant; no penal evil shall befall them; the punishment of their sin has been inflicted on Christ their surety, and therefore shall never be laid on them; and whatever afflictions may happen to them, which have the name and appearance of evil, these work together for their good, spiritual and eternal; so that, in reality, no evil thing, properly speaking, happens to them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill's own gloss on 'no evil happens to the just' concedes real afflictions befall the righteous but reclassifies them as not 'evil' because God overrules them for good — the row's clearest reconciling move against the reality of suffering.

excerpts.excerpt_text: this was stumbling to the prophet, and all good men; and they knew not how, or at least found great difficulty, to reconcile this to the purity and holiness of God, and to his justice and faithfulness …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: A rare PD concession in the commentator's own voice: reconciling God's purity with the wicked devouring the more righteous was a genuine, unresolved 'stumbling' block even to 'all good men,' not a solved harmonization.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats both Proverbs 12:21 and Habakkuk 1:13 directly, supplying the row's harmonizing reading (afflictions are not 'evil' properly speaking) while also naming the felt difficulty in reconciling the two; Haley's Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874) does not index either passage.

link.title: GotQuestions: Why does God allow bad things to happen to good people?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of the row's exact question, arguing present suffering serves eternal, purposeful ends rather than breaching divine justice.
